sections.overview: The European eel is a snake-like fish that spends most of its life in rivers, lakes and coastal waters of Europe and North Africa, then crosses the Atlantic to spawn once and die. Its life cycle makes it a long-distance migrant, and it is now Critically Endangered.
sections.identification: The body is long and snake-like, with the dorsal and anal fins running into the tail fin and no pelvic fins. Females are much larger than males, reaching up to about 133 cm and 6.6 kg, whereas males stop near 122 cm. Eels change form with age: transparent leaf-shaped larvae, then 6–8 cm glass eels, then pigmented yellow eels and finally silver eels with enlarged eyes.
sections.habitat: It is native to the Atlantic coasts from Scandinavia to Morocco and to the Baltic, Mediterranean and Black Sea basins, from streams to large rivers, lakes and brackish coastal waters. It has been recorded from the surface down to about 700 m, and it spawns in the Sargasso Sea in the western Atlantic.
sections.diet: Feeding eels eat a broad range of bottom animals such as aquatic invertebrates, small crustaceans, insect larvae and worms, together with carrion and detritus. The larvae’s food is unknown, since no gut contents have ever been found, and silver eels stop feeding as they start their migration.
sections.behavior: The eel lives on the bottom and is essentially solitary, with no sign of schooling. It hides under rocks and burrows into sand. Silver eels travel roughly 5,000–6,000 km to the Sargasso Sea and, during this journey, move between about 200 m at night and 600 m by day, possibly to avoid predators.
sections.reproduction: The eel breeds once and dies. Spawning is believed to take place in the Sargasso Sea between March and June, but it has never been observed directly. The larvae drift with ocean currents toward Europe for about a year, become glass eels and enter estuaries. The yellow, feeding stage lasts about 6–12 years in males and 9–20 years in females.
sections.ecology: Eels are prey for herons, cormorants and large predatory fish, and their migrations carry nutrients between marine and freshwater ecosystems. They host the swim-bladder nematode Anguillicola crassus. Because they are fatty and feed on the bottom of inland waters, they tend to accumulate pollutants.
sections.conservation: The species is Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (assessed in 2018) and is listed in CITES Appendix II. ICES describes its status as critical: glass eel and yellow eel recruitment fell strongly from 1980 to 2011 and remains very low. In 2020 glass eel recruitment was provisionally 0.5% of its 1960–1979 level in the North Sea index area and 6.5% elsewhere in Europe. ICES advises reducing all human impacts, including fishing, hydropower, pumping stations and pollution, to as close to zero as possible.
